title: With Strict Agendas and Silent Corridors Kazakhstan’s Kurultai Is Muzzling the Press
gist: Kazakhstan's new unicameral Kurultai restricts journalists to agenda-bound questions in a press center, with warnings and six-month accreditation loss, amid a broader press crackdown and Tokayev's apparent moves to extend his rule beyond 2029.

insights.claim: Since Kazakhstan's Kurultai convened in August, journalists may only question deputies and invited officials in the press center and strictly on the agenda; an off-topic question brings a warning, and two violations mean loss of accreditation for six months.
insights.speaker: Catherine Putz
insights.so_what: Narrower information flow from Kazakhstan's legislature raises transparency risk.

insights.claim: Around 40 accredited journalists appealed to Kurultai chair Aibek Dadebay, the former head of Tokayev's presidential administration and leader of the Adilet party, to revise the rules, arguing that agenda-only briefings provide no new information; Dadebay has not responded officially.
insights.speaker: Catherine Putz
insights.so_what: No sign of rule revision yet.

insights.claim: The CPJ's Fiona O'Brien says restrictions on hallway access and non-agenda questions are typical of authoritarian or hybrid regimes that keep an appearance of democracy while controlling information.
insights.speaker: Catherine Putz
insights.so_what: Kazakhstan's governance classification as Not Free by Freedom House affects political-risk assessment.

insights.claim: Journalist Asem Gumarova of Ulysmedia.kz received a warning letter threatening her accreditation after asking about the Caspian Sea drill accident that drowned 14 servicemembers during a briefing on a cybercrime law, and Otkir Kurek founder Nazymgul Kumyspayeva was denied accreditation over an email mismatch.
insights.speaker: Catherine Putz
insights.so_what: Enforcement is already being applied to sensitive questions.

insights.claim: Bazhkenova, former editor of Orda, was sentenced to eight years in prison in August, and KazTAG heads Aset Matayev and Amir Kasenov received 15 months of restricted freedom and five-year bans from journalism in July; CPJ calls the cases politically motivated.
insights.speaker: Catherine Putz
insights.so_what: Press freedom has sharply constricted in Kazakhstan this year.
insights.locator: The Kutultai's media rules merely add

insights.claim: A new constitution effective July 1 and a Constitutional Court ruling say Tokayev may run for another single seven-year term, technically his third, extending potential rule beyond 2029; the CPJ sees press pressure as part of controlling succession.
insights.speaker: Catherine Putz
insights.so_what: Political continuity risk and consolidated control are relevant to long-run Kazakhstan investment assumptions.
insights.locator: The larger political context is unmistakable

insights.claim: The author characterizes the government's view as media existing to relay government-supplied information, with off-agenda questions treated as insubordination.
insights.speaker: Catherine Putz
insights.so_what: Reflects the institutional stance underlying the restrictions.
